blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Explain the three key resources allocation decisions that the economic problem forces on an economy: what to produce, how to produce it and for whom to produce it.

blocks.heading: Three questions scarcity forces
blocks.text: Because resources are finite and wants are not, an economy cannot produce everything, so three key allocation decisions must be made. What to produce: maize meal or blueberries, clinics or football stadiums. How to produce it: by hand with many workers, or by machine with few; in Oshakati or in Vietnam. For whom to produce it: for the households with the money to pay, or spread more widely. An economy run by central officials answers these questions through government plans; a market economy answers them through prices and spending. Whichever system is used, the three questions wait to be answered, because scarcity does not pause for any system.

blocks.heading: Kaoko Juice faces the three decisions
blocks.text: Kaoko Juice in Opuwo has 20 workers, two pressing machines and N$80 000 for the season. What to produce: marula juice sells at N$28 a bottle against N$19 for orange, so the marula line gets the machines first. How to produce it: hand-pressing uses 12 workers and yields 400 bottles a day, machine-pressing uses 4 workers and yields 900 bottles, so the machines run while workers pick. For whom to produce it: supermarkets in Windhoek pay promptly, the stall at the Ruacana gate takes 60 bottles a week, so production is weighted towards the supermarkets. Notice how the decisions interlock: choosing marula (what) made machine-pressing worthwhile (how), and the output went where the money was (for whom).

blocks.heading: Why the decisions cannot be taken separately
blocks.text: The what decision narrows the how decision, because a chosen product limits which methods can make it. The how decision then sets the cost per bottle, and cost limits what can be offered at a price consumers will pay, which feeds the for whom decision. So an economy that changes one answer usually finds the other two shifting with it, and a producer who ignores the link may find its chosen product cannot be made cheaply enough for anyone it hoped to serve.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The economic problem that forces these questions is the subject of topic 1.1; the price mechanism that a market uses to answer them is introduced in section 2.2.3.
